summary: Hannah describes how she started Tiny Post, a monthly snail-mail club, after building a neighborhood farmers market in Austin. She grew the club through TikTok and other organic social posts, then hired help to pack and mail its physical contents. The conversation also covers related letter-club niches, direct-mail ideas, and ways to extend the product. Its strongest lesson for a founder seeking an agent-run business is that the customer-facing storytelling can use software, but making and mailing the distinctive product still takes substantial human work.

speakers.name: Hannah
speakers.description: Founder of the Tiny Project and Tiny Post in Austin.

ideas.name: Tiny Post snail-mail club
ideas.one_liner: Send subscribers a monthly envelope of original art, a recipe, stickers, a paper goodie, and a personal letter.
ideas.business_model: Monthly recurring subscription for a physical mailer.
ideas.customer: People who enjoy art, stationery, tangible mail, creative community, or supporting small artists.
ideas.problem: Subscribers want an affordable way to receive art and a personal, tangible connection.
ideas.offer: A monthly 1 oz envelope with Hannah's art print/postcard, recipe card, usually two stickers, a surprise paper goodie, and a personal letter. The contents change monthly.

price_points.label: Tiny Post subscription price stated by Hannah

pricing.notes: The host suggested testing a $16 tier with a new letter and an archive item; this was a suggestion, not a stated existing price.

acquisition_channels.details: Hannah posted consistently on TikTok, sharing why she started the club, its connection to the farmers market, and the product. A video of her telling her husband about the idea later reached a large audience. She also said unboxing posts from subscribers helped spread the word.

quote.text: And I charged $11 for it. And I just posted it on TikTok. And the first month I got 50 people.
quote.speaker: Hannah

acquisition_channels.details: She started using Pinterest after seeing other people post her work there, and added a signup question to learn whether subscribers came from Instagram, TikTok, Pinterest, or elsewhere.

quote.text: We just added a question of like are you coming from Instagram, Tik Tok or Pinterest, which I would say and then other
quote.speaker: Hannah

acquisition_channels.details: Subscribers shared unboxings and some people discovered the club through their mothers or received a subscription as a gift.

quote.text: people do unboxings of snail mail and they show my mail to other people and then people are interested in that
quote.speaker: Hannah

ideas.delivery: Hannah creates the art and letter, coordinates recipes and paper goods, and packs the envelopes with family and other helpers. The group batches the work during one week each month and ships the letters through the post. Hannah says the personal handling is part of what makes it feel special.
unit_economics_claims: Hannah said postage was 78 cents per envelope and estimated the other hard costs brought the total to about $3.
The host estimated gross margin at about 70% before labor.
Hannah said six people could pack about 1,000 letters in two and a half hours.
Hannah estimated subscriber turnover at about 5% monthly, versus her 10% planning assumption.
The host and guest discussed about 4,100 current subscribers and nearly $50,000 in monthly recurring revenue; the host estimated $25,000–$30,000 monthly profit and Hannah confirmed about $25,000.
ideas.startup_cost: The host described startup costs as next to nothing. Hannah did not give a specific startup-cost figure.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Hannah said she had the idea on a Tuesday and started about a week later. She reported 50 subscribers in the first month.

acquisition.how: Agents could help edit posts, schedule content, answer routine questions, and track referral sources. The most effective content depends on Hannah's personal story, so human input remains important.

onboarding.how: A signup form, payment flow, confirmation, and address collection can be automated, with human review for exceptions.

delivery.how: The art and writing are personal, and people physically assemble and mail the envelopes. Software can manage lists and print labels but cannot replace the core production work described.

billing.how: Subscription payments, renewals, failed-payment notices, and cancellations can largely run through subscription software with occasional checks.

support.how: Agents can answer shipping, account, and product questions from a help guide; personal complaints or creative feedback need a human.

uk_applicability.notes: A UK founder could sell and post a similar monthly letter using UK postal services. The product and subscription model do not depend on US-only rules or platforms.

risks: Packing, postage, and product weight create recurring physical work; envelopes over the 1 oz limit require more postage.
A viral post can create more demand than a small team can fulfill; Hannah closed signups and used a waitlist after feeling overwhelmed.
A waitlist form that does not disclose the price can attract low-intent signups; Hannah said she made this mistake.
The host's gross-margin estimate excludes labor, which Hannah identified as a major cost.
Adding advertisements could weaken the mission and customer trust; Hannah declined an advertising offer for that reason.
A monthly physical product is exposed to postal delays, damage, postage changes, and production errors.

tactics.name: Start with a small local event and show up consistently
steps: Set up a simple first market in a space you control.
Invite neighbors with flyers and offer a welcoming reason to attend, such as free drinks.
Repeat the event monthly so the community knows when to expect it.
Invite small makers and hobbyists to participate, then add activities that fit the event's mission.

tactics.name: Use a personal story as the content
steps: Explain why the product exists and what personal experience led to it.
Show the work and the process rather than only making a direct sales pitch.
Use comments and questions to explain the product to people who have not encountered it before.
Keep publishing and learn from how the audience responds.

quote.text: I shared a lot about why I was doing it and where the idea came from.
quote.speaker: Hannah

tactics.name: Use a waitlist carefully
steps: Use a waitlist if demand exceeds the team's capacity.
State clearly on the signup form that the product costs money.
Tell people when signups will open and how long they may wait.
Measure how many waitlisted people actually buy before assuming the list represents demand.

tactics.name: Protect the one-ounce mail limit
steps: Design each mailer around the weight restriction for the intended postage rate.
Weigh the final assembled envelope before dispatch.

steps: Split the monthly mailer into repeatable steps such as stamping, addressing, inserting, and sealing.
Batch the work into a defined production week.
Bring in and train additional helpers when the original family group becomes overloaded.
Measure letters completed per batch and labor hours before deciding whether machinery is worthwhile.

warnings.warning: Hannah said she panicked when the subscriber count reached 1,200 and closed signups; sudden social growth can outpace fulfillment capacity.

quote.text: And honestly, in October, we had I cut it off because I I truly I panicked at 1,200.
quote.speaker: Hannah

warnings.warning: A waitlist form that does not disclose the price can collect low-intent signups and inflate apparent demand.

quote.text: I just threw up a little Google form like I wasn't even like thinking, but I didn't say that it cost money.
quote.speaker: Hannah

warnings.warning: The monthly product must stay within the weight limit for its intended postage; an overweight issue led to restamping every letter.

quote.text: all the letters ended up being overweight. So, we had to restamp every single letter
quote.speaker: Hannah

warnings.warning: Red wine spilled over letters before a dispatch and created a difficult production problem.

quote.text: one of my best videos was sharing a colossal mistake that I made in November when I spilled red wine over like all of the letters
quote.speaker: Hannah

warnings.warning: Hannah said her labor was a major expense and the workload was concentrated into one week each month.

quote.text: it's too much to put on like one small group of people and it's a lot more work than you would expect
quote.speaker: Hannah

warnings.warning: Hannah declined advertising in the mailer because she believed it would weaken the product's mission.

quote.text: I had a company ask to put advertisements in and I'm pretty sure it would have been a great financial offer. But that completely deteriorates the entire mission behind it.
quote.speaker: Hannah

warnings.warning: A physical product has postage and production costs; the host's 70% gross-margin estimate explicitly excluded labor.

quote.text: 70% gross margins, give or take. Yeah. Without labor.

warnings.warning: Direct mail costs depend on the offer, business, targeting, and postal format; the host did not claim it works for every campaign.

quote.text: It is effective depending on the offer and on the business and the targeting and all that.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

warnings.warning: Hannah said the creative process and influence from similar artists made her cautious about consuming too much competing work.

quote.text: my fear is that I'll take too much of it. And so I work on like also just being like okay I'm staying in my lane.
quote.speaker: Hannah

warnings.warning: The host promoted HighLevel and TK Owners during the interview; these are promotional conflicts for the host.

lessons.lesson: A small local project can create community and a customer audience before it becomes a formal business.

quote.text: I started selling jams in my front yard in my East Austin neighborhood. And it was silly.
quote.speaker: Hannah

lessons.lesson: An authentic founder story can explain a product better than a generic sales pitch and can give an audience a reason to share it.

quote.text: I shared a lot about why I was doing it and where the idea came from.
quote.speaker: Hannah

lessons.lesson: Test a small version of an idea quickly when the cost of trying it is low.

quote.text: I started I think I had the idea on like a Tuesday and we started it a week later.
quote.speaker: Hannah

lessons.lesson: A waitlist only measures buying intent when signups know the offer is paid and understand when they can buy.

quote.text: I didn't say that it cost money. And so I think a lot of people signed up lower intent that it was free.
quote.speaker: Hannah

lessons.lesson: Track where customers discover the product so the founder can distinguish real acquisition sources.

quote.text: We just added a question of like are you coming from Instagram, Tik Tok or Pinterest, which I would say and then other
quote.speaker: Hannah

lessons.lesson: Use customer behavior and feedback to improve the offer; subscriber unboxings showed Hannah what people liked and found confusing.

quote.text: I get to see in real time what they like and what they don't like and what they're confused by
quote.speaker: Hannah

lessons.lesson: A business can stay small and still be meaningful; growth does not have to be the only measure of success.

quote.text: You could stay at 50 subscribers. You could stay at 10 subscribers.
quote.speaker: Hannah

lessons.lesson: Standardize repeatable work and add help when the original team becomes overloaded.

quote.text: This month is the first month we've like really standardized and brought in more people and that has like truly been a huge game changer.
quote.speaker: Hannah

lessons.lesson: Physical details such as weight limits can determine whether a creative product remains economically viable to mail.

quote.text: the weight is what restricts us the most because I can't go over one ounce.
quote.speaker: Hannah

lessons.lesson: Protecting the promise and mission of a product can matter more than accepting every monetization opportunity.

quote.text: the consumers they know what you're doing and that's why they care about it.
quote.speaker: Hannah

lessons.lesson: Be transparent about operational mistakes; Hannah said a candid post about a difficult production failure resonated with subscribers.

quote.text: I don't need to hide this from people and like I can share exactly what made this month a little bit difficult.
quote.speaker: Hannah

lessons.lesson: A founder can try business to learn whether it fits, even if they later return to employment.

quote.text: Even if you end up hating it and you go back to your job, fine. But just learn for yourself if it was for you.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

evidence_quality.rationale: Hannah is a first-hand operator and gives concrete details about subscription growth, packing, postage, churn, and product contents. Some figures are estimates, host calculations, or not independently verified, and the month labels for subscriber growth conflict in the transcript. The host also makes promotional claims and introduces business ideas without operating evidence.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The host ran sponsor reads for HighLevel and promoted TK Owners, a paid or community business resource whose price was not stated.
